newsitem.title: USA: Feb. restructuring eyed for Milwaukee Brewer bonds.
newsitem.headline: Feb. restructuring eyed for Milwaukee Brewer bonds.

text.p: A Wisconsin board charged with financing a $250 million ballpark for the Milwaukee Brewers baseball team is eyeing a February restructuring of $146.7 million of convertible option bonds that were sold in December, a banker working on the deal said Friday.

Neil Flanagan, an associate director at Bear, Stearns & Co, the senior manager on the deal, said the restructuring to long-term, fixed-rate revenue debt was tentatively scheduled for pricing the third week in February with the closing occuring sometime after March 1.
The Southeast Wisconsin Professional Baseball Park District board quietly sold the convertible option bonds December 3 with a mandatory tender anytime between March 1 and December 15, 1997.
The deal, which was rated MIG-1 by Moody's Investors Service, placed the bond proceeds in a guarenteed investment contract provided by triple-A rated Bayerische Landesbank pending the tender.

Flanagan said the restructuring would proceed even if a lawsuit, challenging the legality of the revenue stream for debt service on the bonds, is not resolved. That lawsuit is pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals in Chicago.
He said the district expects to receive a no-merit opinion on the lawsuit from lawyers. He added that talks have been initiated with bond insurers about insuring the restructured bonds.

The lawsuit filed by a group of Milwaukee area taxpayers challenges the constitutionality of a 0.1 percent, five-county sales tax that will be tapped to pay off the bonds. The suit had been dismissed by a federal court judge in Milwaukee and the constitutionality of the tax has been upheld by the Wisconsin Supreme Court.
George Watts, the lead plaintiff in the case, said Friday the district would be "reckless" if it chose to go forward with the bond restructuring before the lawsuit was resolved.
"We really feel we will win this case in the appeals court," Watts said. "Their reckless behavior is only because their case is weak."
The structure of the December debt issue allowed the district board to circumvent plans by Watts and the other taxpayers to file a lawsuit challenging the bond sale.

It also positioned the district to avoid potential problems with the scheduled January 21 reintroduction of a bill by U.S. Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan that would prohibit the use of tax-exempt debt for professional sports stadiums.
